title: Manasseh, Zelophehad's Daughters, and the Forest
summary: Manasseh's western allotment is described, with its clans named and its border set against Ephraim's. The daughters of Zelophehad come forward to claim the inheritance Moses had promised them, and Joshua gives it. Manasseh cannot occupy several strong Canaanite cities in the valleys, and when the house of Joseph complains that its land is too small, Joshua tells them to clear the forested hill country and to trust that they can drive out even Canaanites with iron chariots.
story: Chapter 16 gave Ephraim's land; chapter 17 gives the rest of Joseph's share to Manasseh, whose eastern half had already received Gilead and Bashan (13:29-31). The chapter continues the pattern of chapters 15-16: a gift described, a promise honored, and a failure admitted. Its first story, the daughters of Zelophehad, completes a case that began in Numbers 27 and 36. Its last story, Joseph's complaint, shows a tribe that sees its size as a claim on more land but its enemies as too strong to face. Joshua answers with a challenge rather than a larger grant, sending the tribes to work and to trust.
historical:
Western Manasseh held the northern part of the central hills, including the region of Shechem and the later city of Samaria, and reached toward the fertile Jezreel Valley. The cities in verse 11 (Beth-shean, Ibleam, Dor, Endor, Taanach, and Megiddo) guarded the valley and the coastal road. Beth-shean was an Egyptian administrative center in the Late Bronze Age and into the early Iron Age, and later the Philistines hung Saul's body on its wall (1 Samuel 31:10). Megiddo and Taanach commanded the passes. These strong valley cities were exactly the ones Manasseh could not take (compare Judges 1:27).

Several clan names in verses 2-3 appear outside the Bible. The Samaria ostraca, inscribed pottery pieces from the eighth century BC found at Samaria in 1910, record shipments of oil and wine from districts bearing names such as Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, and Shemida, and also Hoglah and Noah, names of Zelophehad's daughters. This suggests that the clan names became the names of districts in the region. Gideon, one of the great judges, would later come from the clan of Abiezer (Judges 6:11).
cultural:
Inheritance normally passed through sons. When Zelophehad died with only daughters, his daughters asked Moses whether their father's name should vanish from his clan (Numbers 27:1-11). The LORD ruled that daughters could inherit when there were no sons, a significant provision in its world, with the added condition in Numbers 36 that they marry within their father's tribe so that land would not pass to another tribe. Here the daughters return, a generation of promises later, to see the ruling put into practice, and they appeal to it with confidence.

Iron chariots were probably chariots with iron fittings or reinforcements, the most formidable weapon of the plains, where they could maneuver freely. In the hills they were far less useful, which helps explain why Israel settled first in the highlands. Much of the central hill country was still wooded, and clearing forest for terraced farms was hard work. Joshua's command to clear the forest describes the actual process by which the hills were settled.
literary: The chapter has three movements. Verses 1-6 describe the clans of Manasseh and the grant to Zelophehad's daughters, explaining why Manasseh received ten shares west of the Jordan. Verses 7-13 give the border with Ephraim and admit Manasseh's failure in the valley cities. Verses 14-18 are a dialogue between Joshua and the house of Joseph, with the complaint, a first answer, a second complaint, and a final answer. Joshua turns their own words back on them: they say they are many because the LORD has blessed them, and he replies, "You have many people and great strength," so they have the means for both the clearing and the fighting.

outline.t: The daughters of Zelophehad receive their inheritance
Manasseh's borders and the cities not taken

doctrines.note: The daughters of Zelophehad appeal to the LORD's command through Moses, and Joshua carries it out. God's law here protects those who would otherwise be left without a share, and the leaders keep it faithfully.

The house of Joseph believes it is blessed but doubts it can face iron chariots. Joshua answers that they can drive them out. Faith in God's blessing must include trust for the hard work and the frightening enemy, not only confidence about the reward.
The chapter preserves families by name, including five daughters whose names might easily have been lost. Their story shows that the inheritance was meant for every household in Israel.

words.note: Chevel, a cord or measuring line, and by extension a share of land measured out with it. Ten shares, literally ten cords, fell to Manasseh (verse 5). The same image appears in Psalm 16:6, where the psalmist rejoices that the lines have fallen for him in pleasant places.

Barzel, iron. In the early Iron Age iron was still costly and associated with military advantage. The Canaanites' iron chariots represent superior technology, and the house of Joseph fears them. Joshua does not deny their strength; he denies that it settles the matter.

Bara, usually to create, but in one stem of the verb it means to cut down or clear, as in verses 15 and 18, where Joshua tells Joseph to clear the forest. It is a different use of the verb from Genesis 1, and no doctrine should be drawn from the overlap, but it is a reminder that settlement meant hard labor.

christ: The link is thematic. The daughters of Zelophehad, with no brothers and no legal standing by custom, are given an inheritance among their father's brothers because God's word made room for them. The New Testament speaks of believers, men and women alike, as heirs according to the promise (Galatians 3:28-29), with no one's share depending on the usual markers of status. Joshua's challenge to the house of Joseph, that their strength and God's help were enough for a hard task, also echoes in Paul's confidence that he can do all things through Christ who strengthens him, spoken in the context of contentment in hardship (Philippians 4:13).

hard.q: If God was with Israel, why could the tribes not drive out the Canaanites with iron chariots?
hard.a: Verse 12 says Manasseh was unable to occupy the valley cities, and Judges 1:19 says Judah could not drive out the people of the plain because they had iron chariots. Some readers take this as a straightforward military report: Israel's hill tribes lacked the weapons to fight in the open plains. The book's theology adds another layer. Joshua insists in verse 18 that they can drive out the Canaanites despite the chariots, and Judges 2:1-3 attributes the unfinished conquest to Israel's disobedience. So the inability is presented not as a limit on God's power but as the result of Israel's fear and failure to trust. Other readers also note that the book is candid about the gap between promise and possession, which many take as a mark of its honesty.

questions: Zelophehad's daughters asked for what God had promised them. Are there promises of God you hesitate to claim because you feel you have no standing?
The house of Joseph wanted more land but not more work. Where are you asking God for more while avoiding the effort already in front of you?
What are the iron chariots in your life, the things you have decided are too strong to face? What would it mean to hear Joshua's words about them?
